These cases and others since should not be read as stating a rule of 
]aw which prevents every new business from recovering anticipated lost 
profits for breach of contract. The rule is merely an application of the 
doctrine that "[i]n order to be entitled to a verdict, or a judgment, for 
damages for breach of contract, 
the plaintiff must lay a basis for a 
reasonable estimate of the extent of his harm, measured in money". 5 
Corbin on Contracts, § 1020, p. 124. The issue becomes one of sufficiency 
of proof. "The jury should not [be] allowed to speculate or guess upon thi, 
question of the amount of loss of profits." Kezeli v. River Rouge Lodg •
